profile.address: Mitchell Bend Highway, Hood County, Texas, 76048
profile.reading: This is a large-scale Bitcoin mining facility on the Mitchell Bend Highway site in Hood County (Granbury), Texas, run "behind the meter" at the Wolf Hollow natural gas generating station rather than as a conventional leased-power data center. Wolf Hollow itself dates to 2003 (788 megawatts) with a second phase, Wolf Hollow II, added in 2017 (1,115 megawatts); Compute North, an earlier cryptocurrency-mining infrastructure company, broke ground on a roughly 300-megawatt mining facility at the site in 2022 to consume power directly from the plant. Compute North filed for bankruptcy in 2022, and MARA Holdings (formerly Marathon Digital Holdings) acquired the Hood County facility in January 2024, with MARA describing full operations beginning that April. The company reports creating about 19 jobs at the site since acquisition and employing roughly 21 people locally, alongside more than $100,000 in annual community giving to Granbury ISD, United Way, and the local Chamber of Commerce. The facility runs thousands of specialized mining computers around the clock, and its constant cooling-fan noise became the subject of sustained community conflict: in October 2024, Earthjustice filed a nuisance lawsuit in Hood County state court on behalf of Citizens Concerned About Wolf Hollow, identifying more than two dozen nearby residents reporting hearing loss, migraines, tinnitus, and vertigo attributed to continuous mining noise, and separate reporting (including a Time magazine investigation) documented the broader community health fallout. In response, MARA states it has converted about 40 percent of the site to immersion cooling -- a quieter method that submerges hardware in liquid rather than relying on banks of air-cooled fans -- and completed sound-wall construction by November 2024, reporting resulting sound levels of roughly 43-63 decibels versus an 85-decibel legal limit. The facility also participates in ERCOT demand-response programs, curtailing its own power draw within minutes during grid stress or price spikes to free capacity for the broader Texas grid. As a proof-of-work mining site rather than a commercial colocation facility, no square-footage, IT-load, or uptime-certification figures in the traditional data-center sense are published; the facility's relevant public specifications are its interconnected power draw and its noise and demand-response record.

reading.body:
MARA Data Center in Granbury, Texas, sits on what was originally a Compute North project that broke ground in April 2022 with a planned scope of 300 megawatts. Marathon Digital Holdings acquired Compute North's assets after the company's 2022 bankruptcy, and now operates this facility. The operator's current published specification does not state how much of that 300 megawatt capacity is built or operating today, so the site's actual IT load capacity remains unconfirmed.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, but only 18 publish power figures; the state's total published capacity across all facilities is 468 megawatts. This facility does not appear in the published rankings because no capacity figure is on the operator's spec page, placing it outside the 18 facilities with disclosed power.

Without a published power figure, MARA Granbury cannot be read as a constraint on AI scaling at this moment, though its original 300 megawatt scope and current status as an active Marathon facility make it a facility worth tracking for future revision if capacity numbers become public.
